verses.52:13: and he set fire to the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem; and every great house he burned with fire;
verses.52:14: and the whole army of the Chaldeans that was with the captain of the troops tore down the entire wall of Jerusalem all around.
verses.52:15: Now Nebuzaradan the commander of the troops carried away some of the poor of the people, and of the rest of the populace that had remained in the city, and of the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the remainder of the multitude.
verses.52:16: But of the poor of the land, Nebuzaradan, commander of the troops, left vinedressers and farmers.
verses.52:17: Also the bronze pillars that were in the house of the Lord, and the bases, and the bronze sea that was in the house of the Lord, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and they carried all their bronze to Babylon,
verses.52:18: and they carried away the cauldrons, and the meat-hooks, and the psalteries, and the bowls, and the small mortars, and all the bronze vessels that had been in the service;
verses.52:19: and the water jars, and the censers, and the pitchers, and the basins, and the lampstands, and the mortars, and the ladles—as many as were of gold, as gold, and as many as were of silver, as silver—the captain of the troops took away;
verses.52:20: and the two pillars, and the one sea, and the twelve bronze calves that were under the bases, which King Solomon had made in the house of the Lord. The bronze of all these vessels was beyond weight.
verses.52:21: Now concerning the pillars, eighteen cubits of height were in one pillar, and a cord of twelve cubits encircled it; moreover, its thickness was four fingers, and inside it was hollow.
verses.52:22: And the capitals upon each of the two were bronze: the height of one capital was five cubits, with networks and pomegranates upon the crown all around, all of bronze; likewise for the second pillar, and pomegranates.
verses.52:23: And there were ninety-six pomegranates hanging down; and all the pomegranates, one hundred, were surrounded by networks.
verses.52:24: And the captain of the troops took Seraiah the first priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the vestibule;
verses.52:25: and from the city he took one eunuch who was set over the fighting men, and seven men from those who saw the king's face who were found in the city, and the scribe, the commander of the soldiers, who examined the recruits, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the midst of the city.
verses.52:26: Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the troops, took them and led them to the king of Babylon at Riblah;
verses.52:27: and the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death in Riblah, in the land of Hamath. And Judah was carried away from its own land.
verses.52:28: These are the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away: in the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews;
verses.52:29: in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, eight hundred thirty-two persons from Jerusalem;
verses.52:30: in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the troops carried away seven hundred forty-five Jewish persons. All the persons, therefore, were four thousand six hundred.
verses.52:31: And it happened in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth of the month, that Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, in the very year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and brought him out of the prison house.
verses.52:32: And he spoke good things with him, and set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were after him in Babylon.
verses.52:33: And he changed his prison garments, and he ate bread before him continually all the days of his life.
verses.52:34: And his food allowance, a continual food allowance, was given to him by the king of Babylon, appointed for each day, until the day of his death, all the days of his life.

notes.1:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew exclamation of distress (ahah) as a triple cry, "A, a, a" ("Ah, ah, ah").
notes.1:11: Vulgate "virgam vigilantem" ("a watching rod") translates Hebrew maqqel shaqed ("almond rod") by its wordplay sense to preserve the pun with "vigilabo" ("I will watch") in verse 12.
notes.1:16: Vulgate "libaverunt" ("offered libations") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of burning incense or making smoke offerings.
notes.1:17: Vulgate "nec enim timere te faciam vultum eorum" ("for I will not cause you to fear their look") gives a reassuring promise rather than the warning found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("or I will dismay you before them").
notes.2:7: Vulgate "terram Carmeli" ("the land of Carmel") renders Hebrew eretz hakkarmel ("a plentiful/orchard land") as a proper place name.
notes.2:12: Vulgate "portae ejus" ("its gates") reflects a distinct reading of the Hebrew consonants that the Masoretic Text vocalizes as a verb meaning "shudder" or "be horribly afraid."
notes.2:16: Vulgate "constupraverunt" ("have violated") emphasizes moral defilement and dishonor, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has a verb meaning to graze, shave, or break the crown of the head.
notes.2:31: The Vulgate joins "quasi leo vastator" (2:30) with "generatio vestra" (2:31) ("like a ravaging lion is your generation"), and translates Hebrew eretz ma'peliyah ("land of deep darkness") as "terra serotina" ("a late-bearing land"), reflecting the agricultural sense of the Hebrew root.
notes.2:34: Vulgate "in alis tuis" (literally "in your wings") calques the Hebrew idiom for the skirts of a garment. The following clause ("non in fossis ... sed in omnibus quae supra memoravi") is distinctly Vulgate, reading "in ditches" rather than "in breaking in" and expanding "all these" to "all the things that I mentioned above."
notes.3:1: The Vulgate opens with 'Vulgo dicitur' ("It is commonly said"), reads 'mulier illa' ("that woman") rather than the Hebrew "that land," and adds 'et ego suscipiam te' ("and I will receive you") at the end of the verse.
notes.3:2: Latin 'in directum' ("straight ahead") and 'quasi latro' ("like a robber") are Vulgate-distinct renderings where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "to the bare heights" and "like an Arab."
notes.3:4: The Vulgate renders 'voca me' as an imperative ("call to Me") rather than a rhetorical question ("have you not called to me?"), and translates Hebrew "my youth" as 'virginitatis meae' ("my virginity").
notes.3:12: Latin 'sanctus' ("holy") is the Vulgate's rendering of Hebrew 'hasid' ("merciful" or "steadfastly loving").
notes.3:14: Latin 'filii revertentes' ("returning sons") translates Hebrew 'banim shovavim' ("wayward" or "backsliding sons") with a participle emphasizing return; the same phrase recurs in 3:22.
notes.4:6: Latin 'confortamini' ("be strengthened") derives the underlying Hebrew verb from the root for strength rather than "flee for safety."
notes.4:15: Latin 'idolum' ("an idol") translates Hebrew 'aven' in its sense of "idolatry" or "vanity" rather than "disaster" or "calamity."
notes.4:21: Latin 'fugientem' ("the one fleeing") reflects reading the Hebrew noun 'nes' ("standard" or "banner") from the verb meaning "to flee."
notes.4:26: The Vulgate treats Hebrew 'ha-karmel' ("the fruitful land") as the proper place name 'Carmelus' ("Carmel").
notes.4:31: Latin 'propter interfectos' ("on account of those who have been killed") is passive where the Masoretic Hebrew has active "before murderers."
notes.5:3: The Vulgate renders 'Domine, oculi tui respiciunt fidem' as a declarative statement ("Your eyes look upon faithfulness") rather than the rhetorical question found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.5:6: The Vulgate reads 'lupus ad vesperam' ("a wolf at evening") and 'capietur' ("will be captured"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "a wolf of the deserts" and "will be torn to pieces."
notes.5:13: The Vulgate reads 'Prophetae fuerunt in ventum locuti' ("The prophets have spoken into the wind") rather than the Hebrew "The prophets will become wind."
notes.5:28: The Vulgate distinctively reads 'praeterierunt sermones meos pessime' ("passed over My words most wickedly," versus Hebrew "surpass in deeds of evil") and includes the additional clause 'Causam viduae non judicaverunt' ("They have not judged the cause of the widow").
notes.5:31: The Vulgate reads 'sacerdotes applaudebant manibus suis' ("the priests were applauding with their hands"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the priests rule at their direction."
notes.6:1: The Vulgate reads 'Confortamini ... in medio Jerusalem' ("Strengthen yourselves ... in the midst of Jerusalem") rather than the Hebrew "Flee for safety ... out of the midst of Jerusalem."
notes.6:2: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew verb as 'assimilavi' ("I have likened"), reading "I have likened the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman," rather than "I will destroy."
notes.6:7: Following an alternate sense of the Hebrew root, the Vulgate renders 'frigidam fecit' ("makes/has made ... cold") rather than "keeps fresh" or "wells up."
notes.6:14: The Vulgate renders 'cum ignominia' ("with disgrace"), connecting the Hebrew term with shame rather than "lightly" or "superficially."
notes.6:23: The Vulgate reads 'Sagittam et scutum' ("arrow and shield") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "bow and spear" (or "javelin").
notes.7:3: Vulgate "habitabo vobiscum" ("I will dwell with you," repeated in 7:7) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew "I will let you dwell."
notes.7:9: Vulgate "libare Baalim" ("pour out drink offerings to the Baals") uses the plural "Baalim" and the verb for libations, whereas the Hebrew has "burn incense to Baal" (singular).
notes.7:10: Vulgate "eo quod fecerimus" ("because we have done") renders the clause causally within the people's speech, whereas the Hebrew expresses purpose ("in order to go on doing").
notes.7:18: Vulgate "conspergunt adipem" literally means "knead (or mix) fat," a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew has "knead dough."
notes.7:29: Vulgate "in directum" ("directly" or "straight ahead") reflects Jerome's rendering of the Hebrew term for "bare heights" (cf. 7:16 "laudem," "praise," for Hebrew "outcry").
notes.8:3: Vulgate renders "eligent" actively ("they will choose") and construes "quae derelicta sunt" ("that are left") with the places of exile, contrasting with the passive Hebrew "death will be chosen."
notes.8:5: Vulgate "aversione contentiosa" ("with a contentious turning away") reflects a distinct understanding of the Hebrew phrase meaning "perpetual backsliding."
notes.8:7: Vulgate "milvus ... ciconia" ("kite ... stork") assigns different bird species from the Hebrew ("stork ... crane").
notes.8:11: The Clementine Vulgate reads "ad ignominiam" ("shamefully," literally "to disgrace"), where the Hebrew has "lightly."
notes.8:13: A notably difficult verse; the Vulgate literally reads "Congregans congregabo" ("Gathering, I will gather") and "dedi eis quae praetergressa sunt" ("I have given them what has passed away").
notes.8:16: Vulgate "pugnatorum" ("warriors" or "fighters") translates Hebrew "mighty ones/stallions" and refers here to battle-horses, as indicated by "hinnituum" ("neighing").
notes.9:1: In native Clementine Vulgate numbering, 9:1 begins with 'Who will give water to my head' (Saints.Bible 8:23), shifting 9:1-26 one verse relative to Saints 8:23-9:25.
notes.9:3: The Vulgate attaches the genitives mendacii et non veritatis ("of falsehood and not of truth") directly to arcum ("bow"), rather than making falsehood the subject of the following clause as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.9:9: Latin visitare super (literally "visit upon") is a recurring biblical idiom for judicial reckoning or punishment (cf. 9:24, 11:22), corresponding to visitationis ("visitation") in 10:15 and 11:23.
notes.9:10: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew terms for "pastures" and "livestock" etymologically as speciosa ("fair places") and possidentis ("the owner/possessor").
notes.9:11: The Vulgate reads acervos arenae ("heaps of sand") and draconum ("dragons," as also in 10:22), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "heaps of ruins" and "jackals."
notes.9:25: Literally qui circumcisum habet praeputium ("who has a circumcised foreskin"), a distinctly Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew phrase referring to those circumcised outwardly in body while uncircumcised in heart.
notes.10:5: The Vulgate reads in similitudinem palmae ("in the likeness of a palm tree"), taking the Hebrew tomer as "palm tree" rather than "scarecrow."
notes.10:11: The Vulgate renders the closing phrase as de his quae sub caelo sunt ("from these things that are under heaven"), rather than "from under these heavens" as in the Aramaic text.
notes.10:17: The Vulgate reads confusionem tuam ("your shame"), linking the Hebrew word for "bundle" to the root meaning "to be humbled."
notes.10:18: The Vulgate has the passive ita ut inveniantur ("so that they may be found"), where the Hebrew has an active verb ("so that they may find").
notes.10:25: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew terms for "families" and "habitation" as provincias ("provinces") and decus ("splendor").
notes.11:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew word for "streets" as foris Jerusalem ("outside Jerusalem").
notes.11:12: Here and in 11:13, 11:17 the Vulgate translates the Hebrew verb for burning incense as libare ("to offer libations").
notes.11:16: Following Clementine Vulgate punctuation, grandis modifies ignis ("a great fire blazed up") after ad vocem loquelae ("at the sound of speech"), where the Hebrew reads "with the roar of a great tempest He has set fire to it."
notes.11:19: The Vulgate reads Mittamus lignum in panem ejus ("Let us put wood into his bread"), where the Hebrew has "Let us destroy the tree with its bread," that is, its fruit.
notes.11:20: Here alone in chapters 9-11 the Vulgate transliterates the Hebrew title Sabaoth ("hosts/armies") as Domine Sabaoth rather than translating it with exercituum.
notes.12:2: Latin renibus ("kidneys") follows the biblical idiom treating the kidneys as the seat of innermost thoughts, motives, and conscience.
notes.12:5: The Vulgate keeps superbia Jordanis ("pride of the Jordan") literally for the dense, lion-haunted thicket along the river.
notes.12:7: The Vulgate uses the accusative phrase dilectam animam meam ("My beloved soul"), matching the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew construct "the beloved of my soul."
notes.12:9: The Vulgate presents two parallel questions about a multicolored and dyed bird (avis discolor ... avis tincta per totum), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of a speckled bird of prey surrounded by other birds of prey.
notes.12:13: The Vulgate reads hæreditatem acceperunt ("they have received an inheritance"), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew verb that the Masoretic Text vocalizes as "they have worn themselves out."
notes.13:14: The Vulgate reads dispergam eos virum a fratre suo ("I will scatter them, each man from his brother"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I will dash them one against another."
notes.13:18: Latin dominatrici ("sovereign lady" or "mistress") renders Hebrew gevirah, the official title of the queen mother in Judah.
notes.13:20: The Vulgate uses a second-person plural verb, qui venitis ab aquilone ("you who come from the north"), whereas the Masoretic Text refers in the third person to "those coming from the north."
notes.13:26: The Vulgate renders this clause as nudavi femora tua ("I have laid bare your thighs"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I will lift up your skirts."
notes.13:27: The Vulgate divides the Hebrew phrase to read non mundaberis post me ("you will not be made clean after Me"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "you will not be clean; after how much longer?"
notes.14:1: Latin de sermonibus siccitatis ("concerning the words of the drought") literally reproduces the Hebrew idiom meaning "concerning the matters" or "events of the drought."
notes.14:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew tannim ("jackals") as dracones ("dragons"), as in 9:10 and 10:22.
notes.14:13: The threefold exclamation A, a, a is Jerome's characteristic Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew lament interjection, and the Vulgate reads third-person dabit ("He will give") where the Masoretic Text has first-person "I will give."
notes.14:18: The Vulgate reads abierunt in terram quam ignorabant ("have gone away into a land that they did not know"), describing exile, whereas the Masoretic Text speaks of plying their trade in the land without knowing what to do.
notes.14:21: The Vulgate reads Ne des nos in opprobrium ("Do not give us over to reproach") and includes nobis ("upon us") in neque facias nobis contumeliam, differing from the Masoretic Text's "Do not spurn ... do not disgrace the throne of Your glory."
notes.15:6: Vulgate 'laboravi rogans' literally reads "I have grown weary of pleading," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I am weary of relenting."
notes.15:11: Latin 'Si non' ("If not...") reproduces the Hebrew elliptical oath formula ("Surely"). Vulgate 'reliquiæ tuæ' ("your remnant") and 'occurri tibi ... adversus inimicum' ("I have come to meet you ... against the enemy") differ notably from the Masoretic Text.
notes.15:12: Vulgate 'fœderabitur' ("be allied") takes the Hebrew verb in the sense of associating as companions rather than "break" or "shatter."
notes.15:14: Vulgate 'adducam inimicos tuos de terra' ("I will bring your enemies from a land") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of making Judah serve enemies in an unknown land.
notes.15:18: Vulgate 'facta est' is third-person feminine singular, taking "my wound" ('plaga mea') as subject ("It has become to me..."), whereas the Hebrew uses second-person singular addressing God ("Will You be to me...").
notes.16:3: Vulgate 'de quorum stirpe sunt nati' ("from whose lineage they were born") expands on the simpler Hebrew expression "who fathered them."
notes.16:5: Vulgate 'domum convivii' ("a house of feasting," also in 16:8) renders Hebrew 'bet marzeah' (a funerary banquet house or house of mourning) literally as a banquet house.
notes.16:13: Vulgate 'qui non dabunt vobis requiem' ("who will not give you rest") refers in the third-person plural to the foreign gods, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads first-person singular ("for I will show you no favor").
notes.17:1: The Clementine Vulgate reads "super latitudinem" ("upon the breadth"), in contrast to the Hebrew "tablet."
notes.17:6: Vulgate 'myricæ' (plural, "tamarisks") renders the Hebrew desert shrub 'arar' as plural tamarisk bushes.
notes.17:8: Vulgate 'ad humorem' ("toward the moisture") renders Hebrew 'al-yubal' ("by the stream") more generally as moisture.
notes.17:9: Vulgate 'cor omnium' ("the heart of all") and 'inscrutabile' ("unsearchable," creating a wordplay with 'scrutans', "searching," in 17:10) differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("deceitful above all things and desperately sick").
notes.17:10: Latin 'renes' ("kidneys") is the biblical idiom for the innermost mind and affections.
notes.17:16: Vulgate 'te pastorem sequens' ("following You as Shepherd") applies "shepherd" to God rather than to Jeremiah, and 'diem hominis' ("the day of man") reads the Hebrew word for "woeful/incurable" as the word for "man."
notes.18:8: The Vulgate uses the same phrase (poenitentiam agere, "repent") for both the nation's turning from evil and God's relenting of intended judgment (and again in 18:10), whereas the Hebrew uses two different verbs.
notes.18:14: The Vulgate reads evelli ("be torn away") and erumpentes ("bursting forth") in a difficult Hebrew line; evelli corresponds to the Hebrew verb "be plucked up."
notes.18:17: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "east wind" interpretively as ventus urens ("a scorching wind").
notes.18:23: Latin abutor (abutere eis) carries the strong sense "use up, consume, or deal harshly with," stronger than the Hebrew expression "deal with them."
notes.19:1: The Vulgate lacks a conjunction and second verb before a senioribus, reading literally "take a potter's earthenware flask from the elders," whereas the Hebrew means "buy a potter's earthenware flask and [take along] some of the elders."
notes.19:4: The Vulgate reads libaverunt ("poured out libations," as also in 18:15), whereas the Hebrew refers to burning offerings/incense.
notes.19:5: The Vulgate uses the plural Baalim ("the Baals") twice in this verse, whereas the Hebrew has the singular Baal.
notes.19:7: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "make them fall" as subvertam ("overthrow"), linking verbally with subvertit in 20:16.
notes.20:3: Rather than transliterating the Hebrew symbolic name Magor-missabib, the Vulgate translates it directly into Latin as Pavorem undique ("Terror on Every Side").
notes.20:4: The Vulgate places te et omnes amicos tuos in the accusative ("you and all your friends"), rather than the Hebrew dative "to yourself and to all your friends."
notes.20:8: The Vulgate reads Quia jam olim loquor ("Because for a long time now I have been speaking"), whereas the Hebrew means "For whenever I speak."
notes.20:10: The Vulgate reads Persequimini, et persequamur eum ("Pursue, and let us pursue him," linking with persequuntur in 20:11) where the Hebrew has "Denounce, and let us denounce him," and renders Hebrew "watching for my stumbling" literally as custodientes latus meum ("watching my side").
notes.20:11: The Vulgate reads infirmi erunt ("will be weak," vs. Hebrew "will not prevail"), makes "the everlasting reproach" the direct object of non intellexerunt ("have not understood"), and closes with numquam delebitur ("will never be blotted out," vs. Hebrew "will never be forgotten").
notes.21:11: The Vulgate reads the plural 'words' (verba), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the singular 'word.'
notes.21:12: Latin calumniantis (and calumniatoris in 22:3, calumniam in 22:17) denotes one who oppresses or extorts under color of wrongful accusation, rendering the Hebrew term for extortion/oppression.
notes.21:13: The Vulgate reads vallis solidae atque campestris ('the solid and level valley') and Quis percutiet nos? ('Who will strike us?'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'inhabitant of the valley, rock of the plain' and 'Who will come down against us?'
notes.22:6: Latin si non posuero (literally, 'if I do not make') is a solemn oath idiom meaning 'I will surely make,' and inhabitabiles literally means 'uninhabitable' (Hebrew: 'uninhabited').
notes.22:16: In verses 15-16, the Vulgate attaches tunc cum bene erat ei ('then when it was well with him') to the question in verse 15 and renders verse 16 as in bonum suum: numquid non ideo quia cognovit me? ('for his own good; was it not for this reason, because he knew Me?'), differing syntactically from the Hebrew.
notes.22:17: Latin ad cursum mali operis ('on the course of evil work') reflects a Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew word for oppression/violence through the root meaning 'to run.'
notes.22:19: The Vulgate reads putrefactus ('decayed/rotted'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'dragged away.'
notes.22:20: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew geographic name Abarim as a common participle, ad transeuntes ('to those passing by').
notes.22:24: Here and in verse 28, the Vulgate uses the fuller name Jechonias ('Jeconiah') where the Hebrew has Coniah, renders the signet simply as annulus ('a ring'), and reads the third-person pronoun eum ('him') before shifting to second-person te ('you') in verse 25.
notes.23:5: Latin germen justum ('a righteous shoot') and rex ('a king') are lowercase; capitalization of 'He' reflects traditional messianic interpretation (cf. 33:15-16) and is subject to edition-wide policy.
notes.23:6: The Vulgate has the adjective justus ("The Lord Our Righteous One") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the noun "righteousness," and uses the active plural vocabunt ("they will call"). Capitalization of 'Him' reflects traditional messianic interpretation (cf. 33:16) and is subject to edition-wide policy.
notes.23:14: Vulgate similitudinem adulterantium ("the likeness of adulterers") is a distinctly Latin reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a horrible thing: committing adultery."
notes.23:22: The Vulgate has the first-person singular avertissem ("I would certainly have turned them back"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the third-person plural ("they would have turned them back").
notes.23:32: Vulgate in miraculis suis ("by their miracles") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of the false prophets' "recklessness" or "boasting."
notes.23:33: Latin onus (like Hebrew massa) carries a wordplay on both "burden" and "oracle." Vulgate Vos estis onus ("You are the burden") agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic vocalization ("What burden?").
notes.24:1: Latin uses two singular collective nouns, fabrum ("the craftsman") and inclusorem (literally "encloser," used in the Vulgate for a locksmith, metalworker, or setter of inlays).
notes.24:6: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for good," the Vulgate has ad placandum ("to be appeased" or "for reconciliation").
notes.25:3: Latin de nocte consurgens ("rising in the night") here and consurgens diluculo ("rising at daybreak") in 25:4 both render the Hebrew idiom for rising early and acting persistently.
notes.25:14: In native Clementine Vulgate order, chapter 25 continues directly with the cup of wrath (25:14-38; mapped to Saints.Bible 32:15-38, with 25:14 absent in Saints), while the Oracles against the Nations stand in chapters 46-51. Latin servierunt eis, cum essent gentes multae et reges magni literally renders the dative construction ('they served them, though they were many nations and great kings').
notes.25:20: The Vulgate renders Hebrew kol-ha-ereb ("all the mixed peoples") as universis generaliter ("all in general"), and uses the Greco-Latin name Ausitis (terrae Ausitidis) for the land of Uz.
notes.25:24: The Vulgate translates Hebrew ha-ereb ("the mixed peoples") as occidentis ("of the west"), connecting it with the Hebrew root for evening and west.
notes.25:30: The Vulgate renders Hebrew nawehu ("His fold" or "habitation") as decorem suum ("His beauty"), deriving it from the root meaning comely or beautiful.
notes.25:38: The Vulgate reads Hebrew hay-yonah ("the oppressor" or "oppressing sword") as its homograph meaning "dove," translating a facie irae columbae ("before the wrath of the dove").
notes.26:3: Latin pœniteat me mali is literally "it may repent me of the evil," an impersonal idiom rendered here "relent of the harm."
notes.26:5: Latin "de nocte consurgens, et dirigens" ("rising up in the night and dispatching") is the Vulgate's literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom for rising early and sending persistently.
notes.26:8: The Vulgate uses the third-person jussive "Morte moriatur" ("Let him surely die," literally "By death let him die") and third-person "prophetavit" ("has he prophesied") in v. 9, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text addresses Jeremiah in the second person.
notes.26:23: Latin "vulgi ignobilis" ("the lowly common people") expands the Hebrew expression "the sons of the people."
notes.27:1: Vulgate 27:1 names Jehoiakim (Joakim); absent in Saints.Bible ch. 34, which begins at 34:2 (= native 27:2).
notes.27:2: The Vulgate reads "vincula et catenas" ("bonds and chains"), rather than the Hebrew "thongs and yoke-bars," a rendering maintained in 35:10-13 with "chain" and "wooden/iron chains."
notes.27:7: Vulgate reads servient ei ('will serve him') at the close of the verse as well as the opening, differing from the Hebrew reading 'will make him serve.'
notes.27:9: The Vulgate renders "somniatores" ("dreamers"), matching the Septuagint, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "your dreams."
notes.27:10: Both here and in v. 15, the Vulgate reads third-person plural "ejiciant vos" ("they may drive you out," referring to the false prophets), whereas the Hebrew has first-person singular ("I will drive you out").
notes.27:18: Latin "occurrant" literally means "let them meet" or "come before," used in the Vulgate here for urgent prophetic intercession before the Lord.
notes.28:3: Latin "duo anni dierum" ("two years of days") preserves a Hebraic idiom meaning two full years; in v. 11, the Vulgate reads "post duos annos dierum" ("after two years of days") rather than Hebrew "within two years."
notes.28:8: The Vulgate reads "de prælio, et de afflictione, et de fame" ("of battle, and of affliction, and of famine"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text lists war, disaster, and pestilence.
notes.28:13: Following 34:2 and 35:10, the Vulgate renders Hebrew "yoke-bars" as "catenas" ("chains"), producing the distinctly Vulgate imagery of "wooden chains" replaced by "iron chains."
notes.28:14: The Vulgate has "bestias terræ" ("the beasts of the earth") here, differing slightly from "bestias agri" ("the beasts of the field") in 34:6.
notes.29:2: Latin domina ("the lady" or "mistress") refers to the queen mother. Latin faber et inclusor ("craftsman and locksmith") are collective singulars, with inclusor literally denoting an "encloser" (locksmith or metal-setter).
notes.29:10: Vulgate Cum coeperint impleri ("When seventy years begin to be fulfilled") is a distinctive reading differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("when seventy years are completed").
notes.29:11: Vulgate ut dem vobis finem et patientiam ("so that I may give you an end and patience") is a notable Vulgate reading, where patientiam ("patience" or "endurance") stands in place of Hebrew "hope" and finem ("end" or "outcome") in place of "future."
notes.29:14: Vulgate de loco ad quem ("from the place to which") reverses the prepositions of the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("to the place from which"), referring to returning out of Babylon rather than back to Jerusalem.
notes.29:19: The Clementine Vulgate briefly shifts to the third person ("misit," "He sent") after "says the Lord" and renders the Hebrew phrase for rising early as "de nocte consurgens" ("rising by night").
notes.29:23: Vulgate Ego sum judex et testis ("I am judge and witness") is a distinctive reading compared to the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I am the one who knows and am witness").
notes.30:3: Latin convertam conversionem (literally "I will turn the turning" or "reverse the reversal," repeated in 37:18) is Jerome's etymological rendering of the Hebrew idiom for restoring fortunes or returning from captivity.
notes.30:8: The Vulgate preserves abrupt pronoun shifts (jugum ejus, "his yoke"; collo tuo, "your neck"; vincula ejus, "his bonds"; ei, "him") and uses dominabuntur ("will rule over") where the Hebrew has a verb meaning "enslave."
notes.30:10: Stage 1 restored Jeremiah 30:10-11 (absent from Septuagint-aligned ch. 37); its wording in Vulgate 30:10 differs in several Latin phrases (salvabo, terra longinqua, captivitatis eorum, cunctis affluet bonis) from the parallel oracle at 46:27.
notes.30:11: Latin ut non videaris tibi innoxius ('so that you may not seem innocent to yourself') is Jerome's distinctive rendering of the Hebrew idiom for not leaving unpunished.
notes.30:14: Vulgate dura facta sunt ("have become hard," echoed by dura peccata, "hard sins," in 37:16) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which describes the sins as "numerous" or "mighty."
notes.30:17: Latin Obducam cicatricem tibi ("I will draw a scar over you") is a classical medical idiom meaning to close an open wound with scar tissue so that it heals.
notes.30:18: Vulgate in excelso suo ("upon its height") and templum juxta ordinem suum fundabitur ("the temple will be founded according to its order") are distinctive renderings compared to the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("on its mound" and "the citadel will stand in its rightful place").
notes.31:5: The Vulgate reads "et donec tempus veniat, non vindemiabunt" ("and until the time comes, they will not gather the vintage"), reflecting the Levitical waiting period before harvesting new vineyards, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "and they shall enjoy the fruit."
notes.31:7: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb for shouting joyfully literally as "hinnite" ("neigh") and translates "contra caput gentium" as "against the head of the nations."
notes.31:15: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Ramah etymologically as "in excelso" ("on high").
notes.31:21: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew terms for road markers and guideposts as "speculam" ("watchtower") and "amaritudines" ("bitternesses"), connecting the latter to the Hebrew root meaning "bitter."
notes.31:40: The Vulgate reads "universam regionem mortis" ("the entire region of death"), interpreting the Hebrew word for fields or terraces ("shdemot") as a compound referring to death. Native Vulgate chapter 31 maps to Saints.Bible chapter 38 (where 38:35-37 follow the Septuagint sequence relative to native Vulgate 31:35-37).
notes.32:9: The Vulgate renders the purchase price with Greco-Roman weight and currency terms (septem stateres, et decem argenteos, "seven staters and ten pieces of silver"), where the Hebrew reads "seven shekels and ten of silver" (seventeen shekels).
notes.32:11: The Vulgate uses Roman legal terms (stipulationes, et rata, "stipulations and ratified terms") and translates the final phrase as signa forinsecus ("seals on the outside"), whereas the Hebrew refers to the open copy of the deed.
notes.32:17: The Vulgate opens with a threefold exclamation (Heu! heu! heu!) and translates the Semitic idiom non erit tibi difficile omne verbum literally ("no word will be difficult for You," similarly in 39:27), using verbum ("word") in the broad sense of "matter" or "thing."
notes.32:19: The Vulgate reads incomprehensibilis cogitatu ("incomprehensible in thought"), whereas the Hebrew reads "mighty in deed."
notes.32:35: The Vulgate reads ut initiarent ("to consecrate/initiate") their sons and daughters to Molech, without the Hebrew phrase "to cause to pass through [fire]."
notes.33:4: In verses 4-5, the Vulgate coordinates et ad munitiones, et ad gladium with the preceding ad phrases and attaches venientium as a genitive ("the sword of those who come"), resolving a syntactically difficult Hebrew passage.
notes.33:6: Latin obducam eis cicatricem is a medical idiom literally meaning "draw a scar over them," that is, heal over their wounds. The Vulgate also reads deprecationem ("prayer/supplication") where the Hebrew means "abundance," connecting the rare Hebrew term to a homonymous root meaning "to pray/entreat."
notes.33:7: Latin convertam conversionem mirrors the Hebrew cognate idiom (as in 37:3 and 37:18); the Vulgate keeps it distinct from convertam captivitatem ("turn back their captivity") in 39:44.
notes.33:10: The Vulgate translates Hebrew chutzot ("streets") literally as foris ("outside Jerusalem"), reflecting the root sense of "outside."
notes.33:12: The Vulgate's triple genitive pastorum accubantium gregum ("of shepherds of resting flocks") uses the intransitive participle accubantium modifying gregum, whereas the Hebrew uses a causative participle ("shepherds causing flocks to lie down").
notes.33:14: Verses 33:14-26 are restored in native Clementine Vulgate chapter 33 (absent from Septuagint-aligned ch. 40; 33:25-26 were previously stored as unplaced entries).
notes.33:15: Latin germen justitiae ('shoot of righteousness') parallels 23:5; lowercase 'he' preserves Latin case ambiguity (flagged alongside 23:5-6 for human editorial capitalization policy).
notes.33:16: Vulgate 33:16 reads 'Jerusalem' (parallel to 'Israel' in 23:6) and masculine eum ('him', where the Hebrew reads feminine 'her'), with adjective justus ('Our Righteous One'). Lowercase 'him' is flagged alongside 23:6 for human editorial capitalization policy.
notes.33:18: Clem1598-USFX prints holocautomata (variant holocaustomata) and sacrificum (orthographic variant for sacrificium, 'offering/sacrifice').
notes.33:26: The Clementine Vulgate reads "reducam conversionem eorum" ("I will bring back their return"), a literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom for restoring fortunes or returning from exile.
notes.34:5: The Vulgate reads 'sic comburent te' ('so they will burn you'), referring to royal funeral burnings of aromatic spices in honor of deceased kings (cf. 2 Chronicles 16:14), whereas the Hebrew text reads 'they will burn [spices] for you.'
notes.34:9: The Vulgate explicitly adds the explanatory phrase 'id est' ('that is') and the conjunction 'et' ('in Judaeo et fratre suo,' 'over a Jew and his brother'), expanding the concise Hebrew 'a Jew, his brother.'
notes.34:16: Latin 'suae potestatis' ('under their own authority,' literally 'of their own power') renders the Hebrew phrase 'according to their desire' with a Roman legal idiom for legally independent, emancipated persons.
notes.34:18: Following the Hebrew, the Vulgate places 'vitulum' ('the calf') directly in the accusative without a comparative 'like,' indicating either that the covenant-breakers will be treated like the severed calf or identifying the calf with the covenant ratified between its divided parts.
notes.34:22: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew 'without an inhabitant' as a causal clause, 'eo quod non sit habitator' ('because there is no inhabitant').
notes.35:2: The Vulgate reads 'in unam exedram thesaurorum' ('into one chamber of the treasuries'), specifying treasury chambers where the Hebrew simply has 'one of the chambers,' anticipating 'gazophylacium' ('treasury chamber') and 'thesaurum' ('treasury') in verse 4.
notes.35:10: The Vulgate reads 'et obedientes fuimus' ('and we have been obedient'), condensing the Hebrew paired verbs 'we have obeyed and done.'
notes.35:11: The Vulgate includes the possessive 'nostram' ('ad terram nostram,' 'to our land') where the Hebrew reads simply 'to the land,' and renders Hebrew 'Aram' as 'Syriae' ('of Syria').
notes.35:19: The Vulgate explicitly supplies 'de stirpe' ('from the lineage') before 'Jonadab son of Rechab,' clarifying the Hebrew phrasing 'for Jonadab son of Rechab.'
notes.36:10: Latin in gazophylacio ("in the treasury") uses a Greek loanword for the temple and palace office chambers (also in vv. 12, 20, and 21), where the Hebrew has lishkah ("chamber").
notes.36:18: Latin loquebatur quasi legens ("was speaking ... as though reading") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew verb for reciting or dictating aloud.
notes.36:26: Latin filio Amelech ("son of Amelech") treats the Hebrew phrase ben-hammelekh ("the king's son") as a personal proper name.
notes.36:29: Latin Festinus veniet ("will swiftly come") renders the emphatic Hebrew infinitive construction ("will surely come") with an adjective denoting haste.
notes.36:32: Latin multo plures quam antea fuerant ("many more ... than there had been before") differs from the Hebrew reading ("many similar words").
notes.37:4: In this critical text, verse 4 includes the clause concerning Pharaoh's army and the Chaldeans' withdrawal (often numbered separately as verse 5), and Latin libere ambulabat ("was walking freely") renders the Hebrew idiom "coming in and going out."
notes.37:11: Latin et divideret ibi possessionem in conspectu civium ("and to divide a possession there in the presence of the citizens") resolves a notoriously difficult Hebrew clause as a public division of property.
notes.37:14: Latin ipse enim praepositus erat super carcerem ("for he himself had been set over the prison") identifies Jonathan as the warden in charge, whereas the Hebrew states that his house had been made into the prison.
notes.37:15: Latin in domum laci et in ergastulum ("into the house of the pit and into the dungeon") pairs a literal rendering of "house of the cistern/pit" with the singular Roman term ergastulum ("dungeon"), where the Hebrew has plural "vaulted cells."
notes.37:20: Latin excepto pulmento ("besides stew") is a distinctive Vulgate reading for the Hebrew phrase "from the street of the bakers."
notes.38:2: The Vulgate reads 'safe and alive' (sospes et vivens), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'as a prize of war, and he will live.'
notes.38:5: The Vulgate reads 'it is not right for the king to deny you anything' (nec enim fas est regem vobis quidquam negare), whereas the Hebrew text reads 'the king can do nothing against you.'
notes.38:6: The Vulgate treats the Hebrew title hammelekh ('the king') as the proper name Amelech ('son of Amelech'), and translates 'court of the guard' as 'courtyard of the prison' (vestibulum carceris) here and throughout this narrative.
notes.38:12: The Vulgate renders 'armpits' literally as 'under the elbow of your hands' (sub cubito manuum tuarum) and reads 'over the ropes' (super funes) where the Hebrew text reads 'under the ropes.'
notes.38:16: "I will not put you to death, nor will I hand you over" renders the literal Latin conditional oath si occidero ... et si tradidero ("if I put you to death ... and if I hand you over [may God punish me]"), mirroring the Hebrew oath idiom (cf. Isa 14:24, Jer 15:11, Amos 8:7).
notes.38:22: The Vulgate uses an active transitive verb ('they have sunk your feet', demerserunt) and expands 'in the mire' into a double phrase ('into the mire and into a slippery place', in coeno et in lubrico).
notes.39:2: The Clementine Vulgate reads 'on the fifth day of the month' (quinta mensis), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Greek Septuagint read 'on the ninth day of the month.'
notes.39:3: The Clementine Vulgate divides the Babylonian name Nergal-sharezer into two separate names (Neregel, Sereser) in both occurrences and leaves the official titles Rab-saris and Rab-mag untranslated as proper names.
notes.39:4: Verses 39:4-13 are restored in native Clementine Vulgate chapter 39 (absent from Septuagint-aligned ch. 46).
notes.39:10: Vulgate reads cisternas ('cisterns'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'fields.'
notes.39:13: As in 39:3, the Clementine Vulgate divides Nergal-sharezer into two names (Neregel, Sereser) and leaves the official titles Rab-saris and Rab-mag untranslated as proper names; Latin also uses a resumptive double verb across 39:13-14 (Misit ... miserunt, "sent ... they sent").
notes.39:14: In native Clementine Vulgate order, 39:14 follows the restored verses 39:4-13 (absent in Saints.Bible chapter 46, where 46:14 directly follows 46:3).
notes.39:18: The Vulgate reads 'for safety' (in salutem), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'as a prize of war.'
notes.40:1: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew title "captain of the guard" with the late Roman military title magister militiae ("captain of the troops"; princeps militiae, "commander of the troops," in verse 2).
notes.40:5: The Vulgate resolves a difficult Hebrew clause ('while he had not yet turned back...') as a direct continuation of Nebuzaradan's speech: 'and do not come with me' (et mecum noli venire).
notes.40:8: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew gentilics 'the Netophathite' and 'the Maacathite' as a place name ('from Netophathi', de Netophathi) and a patronymic ('the son of Maacathi', filius Maachathi).
notes.40:10: The Vulgate reads 'answer the command of the Chaldeans who are sent to us' (respondeam praecepto Chaldaeorum qui mittuntur ad nos) where the Hebrew reads 'stand before the Chaldeans who come to us,' and renders 'summer fruit' as 'harvest' (messem) here and in verse 12.
notes.40:14: The Vulgate translates with an imperative ('Know that...', Scito) rather than the Hebrew question ('Do you indeed know...?'), and similarly renders the Hebrew question in verse 15 as a negative purpose clause ('so that he does not...', ne).
notes.41:5: Latin squallentes ("disheveled" or "unkempt in mourning") describes the men's disheveled state of mourning, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "gashing themselves."
notes.41:7: Latin circa medium laci ("near the middle of the cistern") reflects the elliptical Hebrew phrase "into the midst of the cistern," without an explicit verb of throwing until 48:9.
notes.41:9: Latin propter Godoliam ("because of Gedaliah") interprets the difficult Hebrew phrase "by the hand/side of Gedaliah," where the Septuagint reads "a great cistern."
notes.41:17: Latin peregrinantes in Chamaam ("sojourning in Chimham") translates the Hebrew word geruth as a participle rather than treating "Geruth Chimham" as a compound place name.
notes.42:10: Latin jam enim placatus sum ("for I have already been appeased") renders the Hebrew verb for relenting or regretting with the language of divine wrath being pacified.
notes.42:12: Latin miserebor vestri, et habitare vos faciam ("I will have mercy on you, and I will make you dwell") uses first-person verbs with God as subject and "make dwell" rather than "bring back," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where the king of Babylon is the subject ("he will have compassion on you and return you").
notes.42:18: Latin conflatus est / conflabitur ("were kindled" / "will be kindled") uses the imagery of a fire fanned or smelted, where the Hebrew verb means "poured out."
notes.42:19: Latin Verbum Domini super vos ("The word of the Lord is upon you") reads a verbless noun phrase ("word") rather than the Hebrew Masoretic vocalization as a verb ("the Lord has spoken concerning you").
notes.43:9: Latin in crypta quae est sub muro latericio ("in the vault that is beneath the brick wall") gives a distinctive architectural rendering of two rare Hebrew terms generally taken to mean "mortar" and "brick pavement."
notes.43:10: Latin solium suum ("his royal seat") renders a rare Hebrew word generally taken to mean "canopy" or "pavilion"; quos abscondi ("that I have hidden") keeps the first-person verb within the oracle.
notes.43:12: Latin succendet ("he will kindle") is third person singular, making Nebuchadnezzar the subject (with the Septuagint) rather than first person ("I will kindle") as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text. Latin amicietur ("he will wrap himself") interprets the Hebrew verb as clothing oneself rather than picking clean.
notes.43:13: Latin statuas domus solis ("the statues of the house of the sun") translates the place name Beth-shemesh (Heliopolis in Egypt) rather than transliterating it, and renders the Hebrew "pillars/obelisks" as "statues."
notes.44:1: The Vulgate reads 'through Jeremiah' (per Jeremiam) rather than Hebrew 'to Jeremiah,' and follows the Septuagint in rendering Hebrew Noph as 'Memphis.' Native Vulgate chapters 44-45 map to Saints.Bible chapter 51 (51:1-30 and 51:31-35).
notes.44:3: Here and throughout the chapter (vv. 5, 8, 15, 17-19, 21, 23, 25), the Vulgate renders Hebrew 'burn incense' as 'sacrifice' (sacrificare), and in v. 23 explicitly adds 'to idols' (idolis).
notes.44:10: The Vulgate reads 'They have not been cleansed' (Non sunt mundati) where the Hebrew has 'they have not been contrite/humbled,' and 'in the law of the Lord' (in lege Domini) where the Hebrew has 'in my law.'
notes.44:12: The Vulgate renders Hebrew 'desolation/horror' as 'a wonder' (miraculum), meaning an astonishing spectacle. Likewise in v. 19 the Vulgate reads 'to worship her' (ad colendum eam) rather than Hebrew 'to portray her,' and in v. 25 uses past indicatives where the Hebrew uses ironic imperatives.
notes.45:5: The Vulgate renders Hebrew 'as spoil/booty' as 'for safety' (in salutem). In v. 4, masculine plural 'those whom' (quos) personalizes the Hebrew neuter 'what.'
notes.46:1: In native Clementine Vulgate order, chapters 46-51 contain the Oracles against the Nations (46 Egypt = Saints 26; 47 Philistines = Saints 29; 48 Moab = Saints 31; 49:1-6 Ammon = Saints 30:17-21 [49:6 absent]; 49:7-22 Edom = Saints 30:1-16; 49:23-27 Damascus = Saints 30:29-33; 49:28-33 Kedar/Hazor = Saints 30:23-28; 49:34-39 Elam = Saints 25:14-19; 50 Babylon = Saints 27; 51 Babylon = Saints 28).
notes.46:15: The Vulgate reads computruit ("has rotted away") where the Hebrew verb means "has been swept away," and uses the singular fortis tuus ("your mighty one") where the Hebrew has the plural "your mighty ones."
notes.46:16: Latin gladii columbæ ("the sword of the dove") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of Hebrew ha-yonah, which can also be derived from a homonymous root meaning "oppressing"; the same Vulgate phrase recurs in 27:16.
notes.46:17: The Vulgate renders Pharaoh's mocking title as tumultum adduxit tempus ("Time has brought tumult"), differing from the Hebrew reading "Crash [or Noise], he has let the appointed time pass."
notes.46:22: Latin quasi æris ("like bronze") is a distinctive Vulgate reading reflecting the Hebrew consonants for "bronze," whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "like a serpent."
notes.46:25: The Vulgate translates Hebrew "Amon of No" (the deity Amon of Thebes) as tumultum Alexandriæ ("the tumult of Alexandria"), reading Amon as "tumult" and identifying the Egyptian city of No with Alexandria; the Clementine Vulgate also literally repeats et super Pharaonem ("and upon Pharaoh") twice in this list.
notes.47:3: The Vulgate reads pompæ armorum, et bellatorum ejus ("the pomp of arms and of his warriors") and multitudine ("multitude"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 47:3) refers to the stamping of the hooves of his stallions and the rumbling of his wheels.
notes.47:4: The Vulgate identifies Hebrew Caphtor (Crete) with the proper name insulæ Cappadociæ ("the island of Cappadocia"). In this same verse, the Latin renders the Philistines with both Philisthiim and Palæstinos.
notes.48:2: The Vulgate renders Hebrew Madmen (often taken as a Moabite town name) etymologically as silens conticesces ("in silence you will fall silent") and attaches contra Hesebon ("against Heshbon") to the opening clause.
notes.48:9: The Vulgate translates Hebrew tsits as florem ("flower") and the following verb as florens ("blossoming"); the Hebrew is obscure and has also been understood as "wings ... fly away" or "salt."
notes.48:31: Both here and in 31:36, the Vulgate translates the Moabite city name Kir-heres etymologically as muri fictilis ("of the clay wall").
notes.48:33: The Vulgate reads Hebrew karmel ("orchard" or "fruitful field") as the proper name Carmel (de Carmelo).
notes.48:34: The Vulgate translates Hebrew Eglath-shelishiyah (often taken as a place name) literally as the ablative phrase vitula conternante ("a three-year-old heifer").
notes.48:45: The Clementine Vulgate reads "de laqueo" ("from the snare") and "partem Moab" ("part of Moab"), contrasting with the Hebrew "without strength" and "forehead of Moab."
notes.49:2: The Clementine Vulgate reads in tumultum dissipata ("shattered into tumult"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "a desolate mound" (some Latin manuscripts read tumulum, "mound"). Native Vulgate 49:1-6 maps to Saints.Bible 30:17-21.
notes.49:7: The Vulgate uses the Greco-Latin geographical name Idumæa (Idumea) in 30:1, 11, and 16 alongside Edom in 30:14. It also renders a filiis ("from the sons"), reading Hebrew mibbənim ("from the discerning") as "from the sons."
notes.49:19: Latin ad pulchritudinem robustam ("to the strong beauty") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew neweh ("pasture/habitation") as "beauty" (as also in 27:7, decori justitiæ); likewise, ad illam ("to her") differs from the Hebrew "away from her."
notes.49:20: Latin si non ... nisi ... ("if not ... unless ...") reflects the Hebrew oath idiom expressing strong affirmation ("surely"). The Vulgate also reads plural dissipaverint cum eis habitaculum eorum ("they will shatter their dwelling with them") where Hebrew describes the pasture being appalled at them.
notes.49:25: The Vulgate reads an active plural without a negative (Quomodo dereliquerunt, "How have they abandoned") and urbem lætitiæ ("the city of joy") without a possessive pronoun, whereas Hebrew (Jer 49:25) reads "How is the city of praise not abandoned, the city of my joy."
notes.49:33: The Vulgate renders in habitaculum draconum ("a dwelling place of dragons"), a characteristic Latin rendering of Hebrew tannim ("jackals").
notes.49:34: In native Clementine Vulgate order, the oracle against Elam stands at 49:34-39 (mapped to Saints.Bible 25:14-19). The adopted Latin text (Clem1598-USFX) prints facum for factum ("came").
notes.49:39: Vulgate captivos ("the captives") renders the object personally, whereas the corresponding Hebrew idiom can mean "the fortunes" or "the captivity."
notes.50:21: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew symbolic place names Merathaim and Pekod as common expressions: terram dominantium ("the land of those who rule") and the imperative verb visita ("visit").
notes.50:26: The Vulgate diverges notably from the Hebrew ("open her granaries; pile her up like heaps"), reading instead "open up so that those who trample her may come out; lift stones from the road and gather them into heaps."
notes.50:39: Latin dracones cum faunis ficariis ("dragons with fig-eating fauns") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of Hebrew terms for desert animals.
notes.50:44: Latin ad pulchritudinem robustam ("to the strong beauty") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew neweh ("pasture/habitation") as "beauty" (as also in native 50:7 / Saints 27:7, decori justitiae); likewise, ad illam ("to her") differs from the Hebrew "away from her."
notes.50:45: Latin nisi ... nisi ("unless ... unless") literally reproduces the Hebrew elliptical oath formula meaning "surely ... surely," leaving the implied consequence unstated.
notes.51:1: Latin "qui cor suum levaverunt contra me" ("who have lifted up their heart against Me") translates the Hebrew phrase leb qamai literally rather than decoding it as an atbash cipher for Chaldea.
notes.51:6: Vulgate "nolite tacere" ("do not keep silent") reads the Hebrew verb damam as "be silent"; the verb can also mean "be cut off/perish."
notes.51:13: Latin "pedalis praecisionis tuae" literally means "the foot-measure of your cutting off," corresponding to the Hebrew "cubit" and evoking the set length at which a weaver's web is cut from the loom.
notes.51:20: The Vulgate reads the Hebrew noun mappetz ("war-club/hammer") as a finite verb ("collidis," "you crush") governing "weapons of war," and uses instrumental "in te" ("with you") throughout the following verses.
notes.51:27: The Vulgate transliterates the Hebrew title tiphsar ("marshal" or "military commander") as a proper name, Taphsar, paired with "numerate" ("number/muster").
notes.51:37: Latin "draconum" ("of dragons") renders the Hebrew word for "jackals" in the Masoretic Text, paralleling "draco" ("dragon") in verse 34.
notes.51:38: Vulgate "excutient comas" ("they will shake out their manes") reflects reading the Hebrew verb na'ar as "shake out" rather than "growl," supplying "manes" for the lion imagery.
notes.51:41: "Sheshach" is the standard modern English form of Latin "Sesach," an atbash cipher for Babylon.
notes.51:56: The Vulgate adds the explanatory gloss "id est" ("that is"), renders the verb for the bows as "emarcuit" ("has withered"), and translates Hebrew 'El gemulot ("God of recompenses") as "fortis ultor" ("mighty avenger").
notes.51:59: Vulgate "princeps prophetiae" ("chief of the prophecy") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has sar menuchah ("officer of the resting place").
notes.52:15: The Clementine Vulgate reads "of the multitude" (de multitudine) here, where the Hebrew word may mean "artisans."
notes.52:18: The Vulgate translates several Temple implements distinctively here and in v. 19, notably 'meat-hooks' (creagras, Heb. 'shovels'), 'psalteries' (psalteria, connecting Heb. mezammerot ['snuffers'] to musical instruments), and 'small mortars' (mortariola, Heb. 'spoons/dishes').
notes.52:23: The Vulgate renders Hebrew 'toward the wind / on the sides' as 'hanging down' (dependentia), and reads that all one hundred pomegranates 'were surrounded by networks' (retiaculis circumdabantur).
notes.52:25: Jerome translates the Hebrew phrase 'who mustered the people of the land' using the late Roman military expression 'who examined the recruits' (qui probabat tyrones).
notes.52:32: The Vulgate reads 'who were after him' (qui erant post se, i.e., subordinate to him) where the Hebrew reads 'who were with him.' Native Vulgate chapter 52 includes verses 2-3, 15, and 28-30 (absent in Saints.Bible parallel numbering).
